lessonTitle: Clinical Negligence, Complaints, Regulation and Candour

blocks.text: A patient returns to theatre after a postoperative bleed that was recognised late. She asks you at the bedside: 'Did someone make a mistake?' Your answer touches three systems at once: the civil law of negligence, the complaints process, and your own professional regulation. This unit separates them and gives you an honest way to respond.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical negligence** is a civil wrong (a tort) in which a patient seeks compensation for harm caused by a breach of the duty of care. The claimant must prove, on the **balance of probabilities** (more likely than not), four elements: **duty of care**, **breach** of that duty, **causation**, and **harm** (damage recognised by the law). A bad outcome alone is not negligence: some complications occur even with excellent care. Rules on time limits and procedure are set by statute and court rules; check current law.

headers: Example of failure of the element
rows: Did the clinician owe the patient a duty?
Almost always yes once a doctor-patient relationship exists
Did care fall below the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner in that role?
A reasonable body of colleagues would have done the same
But for the breach, would the harm probably have been avoided?
The same outcome would have occurred with correct care
Did the patient suffer recognised damage, such as injury, pain or financial loss?
A mistake occurred but the patient was not affected
blocks.caption: The four elements of clinical negligence, each of which must be proved.

blocks.title: Standard of care
blocks.text: The standard is that of a reasonably competent practitioner of the same grade and specialty. Courts have traditionally asked whether the clinician acted in accordance with a responsible body of medical opinion (the Bolam test), provided that opinion is logically defensible (Bolitho). Consent and disclosure of risk follow a separate patient-centred standard. Check current law for the detail.

blocks.title: Analysing a delayed diagnosis
blocks.prompt: A 62-year-old man tells his GP he has coughed up small amounts of blood for six weeks. No chest imaging or referral is arranged. Four months later he is found to have an advanced lung tumour. He considers a claim.

steps.text: Duty: he was a registered patient consulting his GP, so a duty of care existed.

Breach: ask whether a reasonably competent GP, aware of persistent haemoptysis, would have arranged investigation or referral under accepted guidance. If so, failing to do so is a breach; if a responsible body of GPs would also have watched and waited, there is no breach.
Causation: ask whether, but for the delay, the outcome would probably have been materially better, such as an operable tumour. If the cancer would have been equally advanced earlier, causation fails.
Harm: identify the damage attributable to the delay, such as loss of curative treatment, additional suffering or earlier death, and distinguish it from the harm of the disease itself.

blocks.answer: Negligence requires all four elements. Here, breach and causation are the likely areas of dispute, and each must be proved on the balance of probabilities.

blocks.title: Outcome is not the test
blocks.text: Do not say 'it was a mistake' or 'it was just a complication' before facts are known. Describe what happened honestly, say what you do and do not know, and let investigation determine whether standards were met.

blocks.markdown: **Complaints.** Patients and families may complain about NHS care. The usual route in England is **local resolution** with the provider, with the response expected within a reasonable time; if the complainant is dissatisfied, they may take it to the **Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman** (check current NHS complaints regulations, including time limits). Complaints are about the service and seek explanation, apology and improvement; they do not by themselves award compensation. Complaints may reveal concerns that need referral to a regulator or incident investigation.

**Professional regulation.** The **General Medical Council (GMC)** registers doctors and sets standards in *Good Medical Practice*. A **fitness-to-practise** concern, which may come from a patient, employer, police or the doctor themselves, is assessed to decide whether it raises a question of impaired fitness to practise. The GMC may close it, issue advice, agree undertakings or refer the case to a **Medical Practitioners Tribunal**. Sanctions range from a warning, conditions on registration or suspension to erasure. An **interim order** can restrict practice while an investigation proceeds if necessary to protect the public. The purpose is public protection, not punishment.

rows: Compensation for harm caused by breach
Protect the public and maintain confidence in the profession
No action, advice, conditions, suspension, erasure
blocks.caption: Different routes address different questions. The same event can trigger more than one.

blocks.markdown: **Duty of candour.** Being open when something goes wrong is both an ethical and a regulatory duty. The **professional duty of candour** (GMC and Nursing and Midwifery Council joint guidance) requires clinicians to be open and honest with patients when something has gone wrong that has caused, or could cause, harm or distress: tell the patient, apologise, offer an appropriate remedy or support, and explain fully what is likely to follow. In addition, a **statutory organisational duty of candour** applies to health service providers in England for notifiable safety incidents (check current regulations). An apology is not an admission of liability.

items: Recognise and act: ensure the patient is safe and any harm is put right where possible
Tell the patient (or those close to them) promptly, in plain language, about what happened
Apologise sincerely: an apology is not an admission of legal liability
Explain what is known and what is not, and what will happen next
Offer support and a point of contact
Report and record the incident through the proper systems, and cooperate with investigation

blocks.title: Practising candour after a postoperative bleed
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old woman had a laparoscopic gall bladder operation. A postoperative bleed was recognised late, and she required a second operation and an intensive care stay. You were not present at the first operation but are asked to speak to her.

steps.text: First check that the patient is clinically stable, and speak with your senior and the clinical lead so that the conversation reflects the facts known and who should be present.

Meet the patient in a private place, offer to include a relative, and explain in plain language what happened: the bleed, the delay in recognising it and the second operation. Do not speculate about blame.
Apologise for the harm and distress, state what is not yet known, and explain that the event will be reviewed and that she will be told the outcome.
Record the conversation, complete an incident report, give her a named contact, and inform her about the complaints route if she wishes.

blocks.answer: Candour means prompt, honest disclosure, a sincere apology, support and a clear plan, while the investigation establishes whether care fell below standard.

blocks.title: Three systems, one event
blocks.text: A single event can lead to a complaint (explanation and improvement), a civil claim (compensation, requiring breach and causation) and a fitness-to-practise referral (public protection). Candour is owed in all three situations.

points: Negligence requires proof of duty, breach, causation and harm on the balance of probabilities; a bad outcome alone is not negligence.
Breach is judged against a reasonably competent practitioner, with the Bolam and Bolitho principles; causation is tested by whether the harm would probably have been avoided but for the breach.
Complaints seek explanation and improvement, claims seek compensation, and fitness-to-practise processes protect the public; the GMC can impose interim orders and sanctions from warnings to erasure.
The professional duty of candour requires openness, apology, support and explanation when care goes wrong and may have caused harm, and an apology is not an admission of liability.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Bolam test, subject to the Bolitho qualification?

options.text: A doctor is in breach whenever a patient is harmed
A doctor is not in breach if the care accords with a responsible body of medical opinion, provided the opinion is logically defensible
A doctor is in breach unless every colleague agrees with the approach
A doctor is in breach if the patient disagrees with the treatment

questions.correctOptionText: A doctor is not in breach if the care accords with a responsible body of medical opinion, provided the opinion is logically defensible

distractorRationale.a: Harm alone does not equal breach.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: acceptance by a responsible body of opinion, if logically defensible, shows no breach.
distractorRationale.d: Patient disagreement is not the test.

questions.explanation: The Bolam principle asks whether the doctor acted as a responsible body of medical opinion would, and Bolitho adds that the opinion must withstand logical analysis. Check current law, since the position on consent differs.

questions.stem: A nurse administers a medication without checking the patient's allergy wristband, contrary to hospital protocol. The patient is not allergic and suffers no ill effects. Which element of negligence is missing?

distractorRationale.a: A nurse owes a duty to a patient.
distractorRationale.b: The omission could amount to breach of the protocol.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: no damage means no claim in negligence, even though the practice was poor.

questions.explanation: A claim in negligence requires damage. A lapse that causes no harm may still be a patient safety incident and a professional concern, but it does not found a claim for compensation.

questions.stem: A man with a perforated appendix is wrongly discharged from the emergency department and returns later with peritonitis. Expert evidence shows that he would have needed the same operation and would have had the same outcome even if admitted earlier. Which element of negligence fails?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: but for the discharge the outcome would probably have been the same, so causation fails.
distractorRationale.b: A duty was owed on attendance.
distractorRationale.c: The decision may well have been below standard, but that is not the point of failure here.
distractorRationale.d: The patient suffered illness, but it was not caused by the breach.

questions.explanation: Causation asks whether the harm would probably have been avoided but for the breach. If the same outcome would have occurred anyway, the claim fails even if there was a breach.

questions.stem: A poor outcome after treatment proves that the clinician was negligent.
questions.explanation: Negligence requires proof of breach and causation, not just a bad result. Complications can occur despite care that meets the required standard.

questions.stem: A family is unhappy about their father's care and want an explanation and apology but not compensation. What is the usual first step in the NHS complaints process in England?

options.text: Local resolution with the provider, with the Ombudsman available later if unresolved
Refer the doctor to the GMC only

questions.correctOptionText: Local resolution with the provider, with the Ombudsman available later if unresolved

distractorRationale.a: The Ombudsman usually considers complaints after local resolution.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: local resolution is the usual first step.
distractorRationale.c: A claim seeks compensation, not an explanation.
distractorRationale.d: GMC referral addresses fitness to practise, which is a separate issue.

questions.explanation: Complaints are normally resolved locally first and can then be escalated to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Check current regulations for time limits.

questions.stem: A doctor is the subject of serious allegations that raise concerns about patient safety while the GMC investigates. What can the GMC do to protect the public pending outcome?

options.text: Impose an interim order restricting or suspending registration if necessary to protect the public
Erase the doctor from the register without a hearing
Do nothing until the investigation ends

questions.correctOptionText: Impose an interim order restricting or suspending registration if necessary to protect the public

distractorRationale.a: Correct: interim orders protect the public while the case is investigated.
distractorRationale.b: Erasure is a sanction after a determination.
distractorRationale.c: The GMC can act in urgent cases.
distractorRationale.d: The GMC does not fine doctors in this way.

questions.explanation: Interim orders are a protective measure while a case is investigated and are not a finding of impairment. Sanctions after a tribunal range from warnings to erasure.

questions.stem: Distinguish a complaint, a clinical negligence claim and a fitness-to-practise referral arising from the same incident, stating the purpose and possible outcome of each.
markingGuide: Complaint: seeks explanation, apology and improvement; handled by provider then the Ombudsman
Negligence claim: civil process seeking compensation; requires duty, breach, causation and harm on the balance of probabilities
Fitness-to-practise: GMC process to protect the public; outcomes include no action, advice, conditions, suspension or erasure
States that the same event can trigger more than one process
Notes that a complaint does not itself award compensation and fitness-to-practise does not compensate patients
questions.explanation: The three routes have different purposes, decision-makers and remedies. Each can proceed independently of the others, so the outcome of one does not decide the rest.

questions.stem: What is the correct position on apologising to a patient after an error?

options.text: An apology is an admission of liability and should be avoided
Apologising is part of candour and is not in itself an admission of liability
Apologise only if the patient demands it
Only the chief executive may apologise

questions.correctOptionText: Apologising is part of candour and is not in itself an admission of liability

distractorRationale.a: An apology is not an admission of liability.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: candour includes a sincere apology without that implication.
distractorRationale.c: The duty does not depend on a demand.
distractorRationale.d: Any involved clinician has a duty to be open.

questions.explanation: Professional guidance encourages honest apology, and the law recognises that an apology is not itself an admission of negligence. Check current provisions.

questions.stem: The professional duty of candour applies only when the patient asks whether something went wrong.
questions.explanation: The professional duty requires clinicians to be open when something has gone wrong that has caused or could cause harm or distress, whether or not the patient asks. The clinician must tell the patient, apologise and offer support.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is given the wrong dressing product, causing a skin reaction that needs extra treatment. Describe how you would apply the duty of candour.
markingGuide: Ensures immediate care and treats the reaction
Tells the patient promptly and in plain language what happened
Offers a sincere apology, noting an apology is not an admission of liability
Explains what is known, what is not known and what will happen next
Offers support and a named contact
Reports the incident through proper systems and records the conversation
questions.explanation: Candour combines honest disclosure, apology, support and reporting. This keeps the patient informed and lets the system learn from the event.
